To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a second-site enhancers variant of a core/AML1 mutant SL3- 3 virus is highly lymphomagenic, that the tumors it induces are T-cell lymphomas as are wild type-induced tumors, that the new enhancer is genetically stable and that it is not transactivated by A ML 1.

SL3-3, a T-cell lymphomagenic retrovirus, can evolve a more tumorigenically potent variant in mice with a nonfunctional AML1 site.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the enhancer in the pathogenic potential and disease specificity of SL3- 3.
the genetic basis of disease specificity and the role of enhancer structure in retrovirus-induced disease.
the evolution of a virus variant that is more pathogenic and more disease specific than the parental virus.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the SL3-3 enhancer is a complex structure, and that the AML1 site is not the only important factor determining the pathogenicity.

the new enhancer structure represents an evolutionary event during the pathogenicity process of SL3- 3, and that this event is the selection for a virus with a more tumorigenically active enhancer structure, although both core/AML sites I and II have been inactivated.
the AML1 site I-II mutation is a necessary but not sufficient genetic determinant for SL3-3-induced T-cell lymphomas.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the pathogenicity and disease specificity of SL3- 3 can be altered both by mutations in core/AML1 sites as well as second-site alterations in the enhancer.
SL3-3 has evolved a new variant with a more tumorigenically potent enhancer structure during in vivo selection.
AML1 site I is the most important for the pathogenicity and that site I and site I-II mutants can form a second-site variant with increased pathogenicity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the AML1 core/AML1 sites are crucial to the pathogenicity and that the NF1 binding sites are also important for the disease specificity of SL3- 3.
a second-site mutation can be a powerful modifier of disease specificity and that it is possible for an enhancer to be genetically stable during the pathogenicity process.
second-site alterations in the viral genome are a common occurrence during pathogenic processes in vivo and may contribute significantly to the evolution of the virus and its pathogenic potential.
